reason: The sources provide 16 claims supported by at least two different sites, with a strong narrative arc regarding the asteroid's 'sodium tail' twist.
story: Meet 3200 Phaethon, the 'rock comet' that breaks all the rules. Discovered in 1983 as the first asteroid found via spacecraft, this 3.6-mile-wide blue rock spends its life on a roller coaster orbit. It dives closer to the Sun than any other named asteroid, reaching a blistering 1,400 degrees Fahrenheit. For decades, we thought it was a 'dead' comet because it leaves behind the debris that fuels the Geminid meteor shower every December. But things just got weirder. Recent observations from the SOHO spacecraft revealed its 'tail' isn't dust at all—it's sodium gas. Phaethon is essentially a giant rock fizzing under the solar heat like a piece of sodium metal in water. This discovery leaves scientists baffled: if there's no dust coming off Phaethon now, where did the massive Geminid debris cloud actually come from? JAXA's upcoming DESTINY+ mission hopes to find out.
angle: The source of the Geminid meteor shower is actually a blue 'rock comet' that gets so hot its surface belches out glowing sodium gas instead of dust.

claims.claim: 3200 Phaethon was the first asteroid discovered using images from a spacecraft.
The asteroid was discovered in October 1983 using data from the Infrared Astronomical Satellite (IRAS).
Phaethon is the parent body responsible for the annual Geminid meteor shower.
It is named after the Greek hero Phaethon, who was the son of the sun god Helios.
It approaches the Sun closer than any other named asteroid in the solar system.
At its closest approach (perihelion), it is approximately 0.14 AU or 13 million miles from the Sun.
The asteroid's surface temperature reaches approximately 1,400 to 1,500 degrees Fahrenheit (roughly 750 degrees Celsius) during its closest approach to the Sun.
Phaethon has an unusual blue color compared to most asteroids.
Its orbit is highly eccentric and elongated, resembling that of a comet more than a typical asteroid.
It is classified as a Potentially Hazardous Asteroid (PHA) due to its size and periodic close approaches to Earth.
NASA's STEREO spacecraft first observed Phaethon developing a tail in 2009 and 2012.
Recent data from the SOHO spacecraft revealed the asteroid's tail is actually made of sodium gas, not dust.
The current observed sodium tail is insufficient to explain the massive amount of material in the Geminid meteor stream.
Its orbit crosses the paths of Mercury, Venus, Earth, and Mars.
The Japanese space agency (JAXA) is developing the DESTINY+ mission to fly by Phaethon.
Phaethon's diameter is estimated to be between 5.1 and 5.8 kilometers.

disputed: The planned launch year for the DESTINY+ mission is variously reported as 2025, 2028, or 2029; the script should say 'planned for launch in the late 2020s'.
The diameter is reported differently across sources (5.1km, 5.6km, and 5.8km); the script should use 'roughly 3.6 miles'.

There is disagreement on which meteorite group most closely matches Phaethon's mineralogy, with candidates being CI, CM, or rare CY chondrites; the script should simply refer to it as a carbon-rich rocky body.
